name: Beagle 2
short_status: Landed on Isidis Planitia on 25 December 2003, never sent a single bit, and was declared lost on 6 February 2004. HiRISE found it intact on 16 January 2015, panels only partly opened; still silent as of 23 August 2026.
tagline: ESA / UK · Europe · Lander · 2003 · The long occupation Failure

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: A UK-led exobiology lander carried to Mars on the top deck of ESA's Mars Express and named after HMS Beagle, the ship Charles Darwin sailed on between 1831 and 1836. It was designed to look for extinct life through isotopically fractionated organic material on and roughly 2 m below the surface, to search the atmosphere for methane as a possible biomarker, and if possible to attempt in-situ potassium-argon dating of a sample.

facts.label: Mass (sources disagree)
facts.value: Every source agrees the lander itself was about 33 kg on the surface: NASA's NSSDCA gives 33.2 kg at touchdown. The probe as flown is less settled. NSSDCA puts the lander package at 69 kg at launch; the 2017 paper written by members of the Beagle 2 team gives 72.7 kg including the entry and landing systems. NSSDCA also lists a 33.2 kg headline mass. The figure it prints there is the landed mass, and it is often mistaken for the launch mass.

facts.label: Size and shape
facts.value: Per the engineers' own description: a shallow carbon-fibre-composite bowl 0.66 m across and 0.08 m deep, a lid of the same diameter and 0.03 m deep, and four pentagonal solar panels nominally 0.57 m across stacked inside the lid with their rear faces uppermost. Fully deployed the lander would have been 1.7 m across, with the panels at 20 degrees to the horizontal. NSSDCA instead describes the bowl as 0.65 m across and 0.25 m deep.

facts.label: Payload
facts.value: The Gas Analysis Package, a mass spectrometer fed by a stepped-combustion oven system; a Position Adjustable Workbench on a robotic arm carrying stereo cameras, a microscope, Mössbauer and X-ray fluorescence spectrometers, a rock corer-grinder and a lamp; environmental sensors; and PLUTO, the Planetary Undersurface Tool, a self-hammering mole on a power cable that was to crawl about 3 m from the lander at roughly 1 cm every 5 seconds and burrow for a subsurface sample.

facts.label: Planned landing site (sources disagree)
facts.value: The 2017 team paper gives the planned site as 11.60 N areocentric, 90.74 E, at -3367 m on the MOLA datum, on the flat floor of the Isidis basin. NSSDCA's page instead states the target as 10.6 N, 270 W (that is 90 E), about 70 km away. The team figure is the one used in the technical accounts of the landing ellipse.

facts.label: Landing ellipse and the 2004 recalculation
facts.value: At launch the 3-sigma ellipse was 174 by 106 km at an azimuth of 74.9 degrees, an area of about 14,500 square kilometres. In 2004 it was recomputed from the reconstructed Mars Express trajectory and Monte Carlo modelling to semi-axes of 28.5 by 3.8 km, that is 57 by 7.6 km, around a nominal point of 90.50 E, 11.53 N. That recalculation, plus HiRISE imaging the region at 30 cm per pixel from 2006, is the reason the lander was ever found.

facts.label: No entry, descent and landing telemetry
facts.value: Beagle 2 carried no system to transmit during entry, descent and landing. Nothing was positioned to receive such a signal: Mars Express was performing its own orbit insertion, Mars Odyssey was committed to Mars Exploration Rover entry operations, and the Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank, acting as a direct-to-Earth listening station, was not in view. So no such system was built. This single decision is why the failure went unexplained for eleven years.

facts.label: Entry and landing times (sources disagree)
facts.value: All times UTC. The team paper gives atmospheric entry at 02:51:22 on 25 December 2003, with touchdown about eight minutes later and first data expected via Mars Odyssey at 05:25. NSSDCA gives landing at about 02:54 and the first Odyssey opportunity at about 05:30. Aerodynamic deceleration was designed to start at 5.6 km/s; NSSDCA describes entry at over 20,000 km/h, which is the same speed expressed differently.

facts.label: The silence and the search
facts.value: Nothing was heard on the first Odyssey pass or any later one. The Lovell Telescope tried on 25, 26 and 27 December 2003, the last attempt jointly with the Stanford radio telescope. Over the following four months 24 contact attempts in total were made through Mars Odyssey and Mars Express. Not one produced a carrier, a fragment or any signal at all.

facts.label: Declared lost
facts.value: The Beagle 2 Management Board met in London on Friday 6 February 2004 and declared the lander lost. On 11 February 2004 UK Science Minister Lord Sainsbury and ESA announced a joint ESA/UK Commission of Inquiry, chaired by ESA Inspector General René Bonnefoy with David Link MBE as UK deputy chairman, with terms of reference covering both technical issues and programmatics.

facts.label: What the inquiry concluded
facts.value: No single technical failure or shortcoming was unambiguously identified, though a few credible causes were highlighted. The report was submitted to the UK Minister for Science and Innovation and ESA's Director General on 21 April 2004 and accepted; its 19 recommendations to the British authorities and ESA were presented at a joint ESA/BNSC press conference in London on 24 May 2004. ESA's release goes no further than saying the Board made clear that there were programmatic and organisational reasons which significantly increased the risk of failure. The specific finding that Beagle 2 had been treated as a scientific instrument rather than as a spacecraft in its own right comes from the full report published in February 2005. The 2004 recommendations do not contain it.

facts.label: Cost, and the funding verdict
facts.value: There is no audited public figure for what Beagle 2 cost. NSSDCA states the exact cost is not known and that most estimates give a range of £40 million to £50 million, roughly $65 million to $80 million at the time; the Science Museum calls it the £45 million Beagle 2 spacecraft. Other figures circulate, higher and lower, because they measure different things: early estimates, the UK government's share, build cost and total programme cost. The Commission of Inquiry's full report, published on 3 February 2005, was less concerned with the total than with the timing. ESA's peer review had approved Beagle 2 on condition that it be fully funded from the outset; that condition was never met, and the lack of guaranteed early funding is described as having seriously hindered the orderly build-up of the project engineering team. The report also concluded that Beagle 2 should have been recognised as a complex, innovative spacecraft needing management by an organisation with relevant experience, which was likely beyond the capability of a university-led group.

facts.label: Hirst, Blur and the money problem
facts.value: Unable to raise cash easily, Pillinger raised profile. He enlisted Damien Hirst to use his spot motif as the instrument calibration chart that the cameras and spectrometers would have photographed on Mars, and pressed Dave Rowntree and Alex James of Blur until they agreed to promote the mission and compose Beagle 2's call sign. Neither the painting nor the tune was ever seen or heard from the surface.

facts.label: The 2005 false alarm
facts.value: On 21 December 2005 ESA reported that the Beagle 2 team believed it had possible evidence for the lander's location in Mars Global Surveyor camera images, centred on a crater near the planned landing site; ESA's Director of Science David Southwood said it would be good news for everyone involved if it turned out to be a definitive sighting. It did not hold up. When MRO's far sharper HiRISE camera imaged the same crater in February 2007, nothing inside it could be reconciled with Beagle 2 hardware, and the object identified in 2015 is not in a crater at all.

facts.label: Found
facts.value: Announced on 16 January 2015. Michael Croon, a former member of ESA's Mars Express operations team, identified a gap in HiRISE coverage, requested an image through the HiWish public targeting programme (ESP_037145_1915, acquired 29 June 2014), and in November 2014 flagged a candidate in it. The clinching colour observation, ESP_039308_1915, was taken on 15 December 2014 at 28.2 cm per pixel from an altitude of 276.4 km, resolving objects about 85 cm across. Croon is listed on the resulting paper simply as a citizen scientist.

facts.label: How many solar panels opened
facts.value: The answer has moved. ESA's January 2015 announcement described only one, two or at most three of the four panels as open. In November 2016 a De Montfort University and University of Leicester reflection-analysis study, matching a 3D model's simulated glints against raw HiRISE frames, concluded that at least three had deployed, and attributed the silence to the fourth panel failing to unfold correctly and blocking the antenna. The 2017 paper says at least the lid and panels one to three could have deployed and possibly all of them, and adds that if all four opened then damage to the antenna system must also be part of the explanation.

timeline: Colin Pillinger of the Open University persuades ESA to carry a British-built lander on Mars Express, then starts hunting for the money to build it, recruiting Damien Hirst for the calibration target and Dave Rowntree and Alex James of Blur to promote the mission.
Mars Express launches from Baikonur on a Soyuz with Beagle 2 bolted to its top deck.

08:31 UTC: Beagle 2 is spring-ejected onto a ballistic trajectory. It has no propulsion, no attitude control and no radio it can use, and coasts for close to six days. All pre-ejection telemetry showed the probe in good health.

Entry is expected at 02:51:22 UTC at 5.6 km/s, with airbag-cushioned touchdown roughly eight minutes later (NSSDCA gives about 02:54). Nothing on Earth or in Mars orbit is listening, by design. The first call home, due through Mars Odyssey at 05:25 UTC, never arrives. The Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank listens for surface transmissions directly on 25, 26 and 27 December, the last attempt alongside the Stanford radio telescope, and hears nothing.

After 24 contact attempts over four months through Mars Odyssey and Mars Express, the Beagle 2 Management Board meets in London and declares the lander lost. ESA and Lord Sainsbury announce a joint Commission of Inquiry five days later.

The Commission of Inquiry's 19 recommendations are presented at a joint ESA/BNSC press conference in London, five days after ESA's release announcing them. No single technical failure is identified; the weight of the finding falls on programmatic and organisational causes.
The full inquiry report is published, concluding that ESA should not have confirmed Beagle 2's selection when the peer review committee's condition of guaranteed full funding had not been met.

Pillinger presents processed Mars Global Surveyor camera images of a crater inside the landing ellipse and argues Beagle 2 may be in it. When MRO's far sharper HiRISE camera photographs the same crater in February 2007, nothing inside it can be reconciled with Beagle 2 hardware.
Colin Pillinger dies in May, a decade after the landing and before any image of Beagle 2 had been found. He never learns that it made it down.

ESA, NASA and the UK announce that Beagle 2 has been identified in HiRISE imagery in Isidis Planitia, about 5 km from the centre of the expected landing area, partially deployed. The entry, descent and landing sequence had worked.

Reflection analysis at De Montfort and Leicester concludes at least three of four panels opened, and the peer-reviewed identification paper follows in Royal Society Open Science, fixing the position at 90.43139 E, 11.52879 N and dedicating itself to the late Colin Pillinger.

The UK Space Agency announces 13 commemorative red plaques to be unveiled at Beagle 2 sites across the UK, from the National Space Centre in Leicester to Airbus in Stevenage, the Open University and Jodrell Bank.

The clinching colour HiRISE observation of 15 December 2014, in which a bright feature a couple of metres across in Isidis Planitia is labelled as Beagle 2, with a 10 m scale bar for reference.
